pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: You run `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml`. Does that create a pod? Walk me through what actually happens, and what keeps happening afterwards.
expected_points: apply records desired state with the API server, which stores it (etcd); it does not create anything itself
controllers run a loop: observe actual, compare with desired, act to close the gap
the ReplicaSet controller creates pods, the scheduler assigns nodes, the kubelet starts containers — each independently, all talking only to the API server
level-triggered, not event-driven: the comparison repeats forever, so drift and missed events self-correct
spec is yours, status is written by controllers

questions.prompt: What is a pod, and why do you almost never write a `kind: Pod` manifest? Where do ReplicaSets fit in?
expected_points: a pod is one or more containers scheduled together, sharing a network namespace (localhost) and IP
a pod is mortal and unrepairable: if its node dies it is gone, and nothing recreates it
a Deployment records the wish, so a controller recreates pods from the template
the Deployment manages ReplicaSets; the ReplicaSet keeps N pods matching its selector alive
usually one container per pod; sidecars are the exception

questions.prompt: Every pod is Running but the Service serves nothing. How does a Service find pods in the first place, and how would you diagnose this?
expected_points: nothing references anything by name — a selector matches labels on the pod template
a controller writes matching Ready pods' IPs into an EndpointSlice; kube-proxy programs forwarding rules
a selector that matches nothing is not an error anywhere: everything looks healthy
check kubectl get endpointslices, then compare the Service selector with the pod template labels
other cause: pods Running but not Ready, so they are excluded from endpoints

questions.prompt: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer — what does each add, and which did you pick for `timesvc` and why?
expected_points: cumulative: LoadBalancer is a NodePort is a ClusterIP
ClusterIP is an in-cluster virtual IP plus DNS; the default and right for internal callers
NodePort opens the same port on every node (30000-32767)
LoadBalancer provisions real cloud infrastructure per Service, which is why ingress usually fronts many ClusterIPs
kubectl port-forward reaches a ClusterIP from a laptop without changing the type

questions.prompt: In your manifests, name every place a port number appears and say what each one means. What happens if you omit `targetPort`?
expected_points: containerPort documents the port the process binds (8080, because non-root cannot bind below 1024)
Service port is what callers dial on the Service
targetPort is the port on the pod that traffic is forwarded to; it may be the container port's name
omitting targetPort defaults it to port, not to the container port — a silent forward to a closed port
a mismatch produces connection refused with healthy-looking endpoints

questions.prompt: One pod is in ImagePullBackOff and another in CrashLoopBackOff. What do you run first for each, and what would you expect to find?
expected_points: describe first and read the Events at the bottom — they are written by the component that made the decision
ImagePullBackOff: registry/tag typo, missing credentials, or with kind an image that only exists in the local Docker daemon (kind load docker-image)
CrashLoopBackOff: the process itself is exiting; read kubectl logs, with --previous because the crashed instance holds the interesting output
the kubelet restarts with exponential backoff, so the state is a symptom, not the cause

questions.prompt: You rebuild the image, push it under the same `:latest` tag, and re-apply. Nothing happens. Why? And what does `kubectl rollout undo` actually do?
expected_points: a rollout only starts when the pod template changes; an identical template means no new ReplicaSet
pin tags (or deploy by digest) so the template changes when the code does
undo scales an old ReplicaSet back up — fast, and limited by revisionHistoryLimit
maxUnavailable: 0 with maxSurge: 1 creates the replacement before removing anything

questions.prompt: What does putting everything in a `timesvc` namespace actually give you, and what does it not give you?
expected_points: a name scope: two teams can each own a Service called api
a handle for quotas, RBAC and kubectl delete namespace
not a network boundary — pods across namespaces reach each other unless a NetworkPolicy says otherwise
not a security boundary by itself
cross-namespace DNS is name.namespace.svc.cluster.local
